concepts.def: A reactant that forms a new covalent bond to its reaction partner (the electrophile) by donating BOTH bonding electrons. A nucleophile is electron-rich and has an electron pair available to donate, usually a lone pair. Nucleophiles may be negatively charged (OH⁻, CN⁻, Cl⁻, Br⁻) or neutral molecules with a lone pair (H₂O, NH₃); a charge is not required.

A reaction in which a nucleophile donates an electron pair to form a new bond to a carbon atom as another bond to that carbon breaks, releasing a leaving group. For a halogenoalkane: R–X + Nu⁻ → R–Nu + X⁻, e.g. CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + Br⁻. The nucleophile bonds to the carbon atom, which carries a partial positive charge because the halogen is more electronegative.

The atom or group that departs when a bond breaks during a substitution, taking BOTH electrons of that bond with it. In the substitution of a halogenoalkane the leaving group is the halide ion, X⁻ (Cl⁻, Br⁻ or I⁻).

Breaking of a covalent bond in which both bonding electrons remain with one of the two fragments. When a neutral molecule breaks this way, the fragment that takes the pair becomes negatively charged and the other becomes positively charged, so two ions form: H–Br → H⁺ + Br⁻. The more electronegative atom usually takes the pair.

Breaking of a covalent bond in which each fragment keeps one of the two bonding electrons, forming two radicals (e.g. Br–Br → 2Br•, as in radical substitution under UV light). It is the contrast to heterolytic fission and is shown with fish-hook (single-headed) arrows.

A double-headed arrow showing the movement of an ELECTRON PAIR, never of an atom or ion. It starts at the source of the pair (a lone pair or a bond) and ends where the pair goes (an atom, to form a lone pair or a new bond). For H–Cl → H⁺ + Cl⁻ the arrow starts at the H–Cl bond and ends on Cl.

A reactant that forms a new covalent bond to its reaction partner (the nucleophile) by ACCEPTING both bonding electrons from that partner. Electrophiles are electron-deficient; they may be positively charged (H⁺, NO₂⁺) or neutral molecules (HBr, Br₂). A positive charge is not required.

The typical reaction of alkenes. The C=C double bond is a region of high electron density, so it attracts electrophiles; the reagent adds across the double bond, which becomes a single bond, and no by-product is formed (all the atoms of the reagent end up in the addition product). The C=C bond is STRONGER overall than a C–C single bond; its reactivity comes from the accessible, electron-rich second bond, not from weakness.

concepts.term: Reactions of alkenes with water, halogens and hydrogen halides
concepts.def: Water (as steam, with an acid catalyst such as phosphoric acid) adds H and OH to form an alcohol: CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O → CH₃CH₂OH. A halogen adds one halogen atom to each carbon to form a dihalogenoalkane: CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → CH₂BrCH₂Br; the orange-brown colour of bromine disappears, which is used as a test for C=C. A hydrogen halide adds H and X to form a halogenoalkane: CH₂=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃CH₂Br.

A Lewis acid is an electron-pair acceptor; a Lewis base is an electron-pair donor. The definitions need no hydrogen: BF₃ and AlCl₃ are Lewis acids because B and Al have an incomplete valence shell, and H⁺ is a Lewis acid when it accepts a lone pair from H₂O to form H₃O⁺. In organic chemistry the C=C bond of an alkene acts as a Lewis base toward H⁺.

A covalent bond in which both shared electrons come from the same atom (a Lewis base donating a lone pair to a Lewis acid). Once formed it is a covalent bond like any other: in NH₄⁺ all four N–H bonds are identical. In the Lewis formula of H₃N–BF₃ the N–B bond is a coordination bond, formed from the nitrogen lone pair.

concepts.term: Nucleophiles as Lewis bases, electrophiles as Lewis acids
concepts.def: Every nucleophile donates an electron pair, so it is a Lewis base; every electrophile accepts an electron pair, so it is a Lewis acid. When OH⁻ attacks CH₃CH₂Br, OH⁻ is both the nucleophile and the Lewis base; when an alkene reacts with H⁺, H⁺ is both the electrophile and the Lewis acid.

A ligand is a molecule or ion with a lone pair that it donates to a transition element cation, forming a coordination bond. Ligands may be neutral (H₂O, NH₃) or negative (Cl⁻, CN⁻). A complex ion is the central cation together with its ligands, written in square brackets, e.g. [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺, [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻, [CoCl₄]²⁻.

The charge on a complex ion is the sum of the charge on the metal ion and the charges on all the ligands. Neutral ligands add nothing. Examples: Fe³⁺ + 6CN⁻ gives (+3) + 6(−1) = −3, [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻; Cu²⁺ + 4NH₃ + 2H₂O gives +2, [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺; Co²⁺ + 4Cl⁻ gives −2, [CoCl₄]²⁻.

Bimolecular nucleophilic substitution, typical of primary halogenoalkanes. It is concerted: in ONE step the nucleophile's lone pair forms the new bond to carbon while the C–X bond breaks, through a transition state (not an intermediate). The nucleophile attacks from the side opposite the halogen (backside attack). Rate = k[halogenoalkane][nucleophile]. The '2' refers to the two species in the rate-determining step, not to the number of steps.

Unimolecular nucleophilic substitution, typical of tertiary halogenoalkanes. It has TWO steps: (1) slow heterolytic fission of C–X, forming a carbocation and X⁻; (2) fast attack on the carbocation by the nucleophile. Rate = k[halogenoalkane]. Tertiary halogenoalkanes react this way because the tertiary carbocation is stabilized by three alkyl groups and the alkyl groups hinder backside attack. Secondary halogenoalkanes can react by both SN1 and SN2.

concepts.term: Stereospecific nature of SN2 (inversion of configuration)
concepts.def: Because the nucleophile attacks from the side opposite the leaving group, the other three groups on the carbon turn inside out, like an umbrella in the wind. When the carbon is a chiral centre, one enantiomer of the halogenoalkane gives one enantiomer of the product, with the configuration inverted. SN2 is therefore stereospecific.

An ion with a positively charged carbon atom that has only three bonds and six outer electrons, e.g. (CH₃)₃C⁺. It is an intermediate in SN1 reactions and in electrophilic addition. It is planar around the positive carbon. Carbocations are classed as primary, secondary or tertiary by the number of alkyl groups on the positive carbon.

concepts.term: Effect of the halogen on the rate of substitution
concepts.def: For otherwise identical halogenoalkanes, the rate of substitution increases in the order chloroalkane < bromoalkane < iodoalkane. The C–X bond enthalpy decreases from C–Cl to C–Br to C–I, so the C–I bond is broken most easily and iodide is the best leaving group. Bond strength, not bond polarity, is the deciding factor: C–Cl is the most polar of the three but reacts slowest.

concepts.term: Mechanism of addition of a halogen
concepts.def: As Br₂ approaches the electron-rich C=C bond, the Br–Br electron pair is repelled, inducing a dipole (Brδ+–Brδ−). A curly arrow goes from the C=C bond to the Brδ+ atom and one from the Br–Br bond to the Brδ− atom, forming a carbocation and Br⁻. Br⁻ then donates a lone pair to the positive carbon (curly arrow from Br⁻ to C⁺), giving CH₂BrCH₂Br. (The IB treatment shows a carbocation intermediate; a cyclic bromonium ion is a more accurate description, beyond the guide.)

concepts.term: Mechanism of addition of a hydrogen halide
concepts.def: H–Br is polar, Hδ+–Brδ−. A curly arrow goes from the C=C bond to the H atom and one from the H–Br bond to the Br atom, giving a carbocation (CH₃CH₂⁺ from ethene) and Br⁻. Br⁻ then donates a lone pair to the positive carbon, giving CH₃CH₂Br.

concepts.term: Mechanism of acid-catalysed addition of water
concepts.def: The C=C bond donates its electron pair to H⁺ (from the acid catalyst, present as H₃O⁺), forming a carbocation. A lone pair on the O atom of H₂O forms a bond to the positive carbon, and the resulting protonated alcohol loses H⁺, which regenerates the catalyst: CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O → CH₃CH₂OH.

Stability order: tertiary > secondary > primary. Alkyl groups are electron-releasing (positive inductive effect): each alkyl group pushes electron density toward the positive carbon, spreading its charge. The more alkyl groups on the positive carbon, the more stable the carbocation and the more readily it forms.

concepts.term: Major product with an unsymmetrical alkene
concepts.def: When HX or H₂O adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, H adds to the carbon atom that already has MORE hydrogen atoms, so that the more stable (more substituted) carbocation forms; X or OH then bonds to that carbon. CH₃CH=CH₂ + HBr gives mainly 2-bromopropane via CH₃CH⁺CH₃; (CH₃)₂C=CH₂ + H₂O gives mainly 2-methylpropan-2-ol via (CH₃)₃C⁺. This outcome is known as Markovnikov's rule.

Benzene reacts with electrophiles by substitution, not addition, because substitution keeps the stable delocalized ring of π electrons in the product. Mechanism with a charged electrophile E⁺: a curly arrow from the delocalized π electrons to E⁺ forms a C–E bond and a positively charged intermediate in which the delocalization is partly broken; a curly arrow from the C–H bond into the ring then removes H⁺ and restores the delocalized ring: C₆H₆ + E⁺ → C₆H₅E + H⁺.

mcqs.q: Which statement describes how a nucleophile forms a new bond to its reaction partner?
options: It donates both electrons of the new covalent bond.
It accepts the two electrons of the new covalent bond.
It gives one electron, and its partner gives the other.
It transfers electrons, forming an ionic bond.
mcqs.specStatementText: A nucleophile is a reactant that forms a bond to its reaction partner (the electrophile) by donating both bonding electrons.
mcqs.explain: A nucleophile is an electron-pair donor: it supplies both electrons of the new bond, usually from a lone pair, and the electrophile supplies none.
rationales: A nucleophile is an electron-pair donor: it supplies both electrons of the new bond, usually from a lone pair, and the electrophile supplies none.
Accepting the pair is what an electrophile does. 'Nucleophile' means nucleus-seeking: it is the electron-rich partner and donates the pair.
That is how a covalent bond is pictured in dot-and-cross diagrams such as H₂, but in a nucleophile–electrophile reaction the nucleophile supplies both electrons of the new bond.
'Donate' here means supply for sharing. The pair ends up shared between the two atoms, so the new bond is covalent (e.g. the C–O bond in an alcohol), not ionic.

mcqs.q:
2-bromo-2-methylpropane reacts with water:
(CH₃)₃CBr + H₂O → (CH₃)₃COH + HBr
Which reactant acts as the nucleophile, and why?
options: Neither, as neither reactant carries a negative charge
(CH₃)₃CBr, as its C atom accepts a pair of electrons
H₂O, as its O atom and the C atom each give one electron
H₂O, as a lone pair on its O atom forms the new bond to carbon
mcqs.specStatementText: A nucleophile is a reactant that forms a bond to its reaction partner (the electrophile) by donating both bonding electrons.
mcqs.explain: The O atom of water has lone pairs; one is donated to the electron-deficient carbon atom, forming the C–O bond of the alcohol. A neutral molecule can be a nucleophile.
rationales: A nucleophile needs an electron pair to donate, not a negative charge. Both reactants are neutral, but a lone pair on the O atom of H₂O forms the new C–O bond, so water is the nucleophile.
Accepting an electron pair is the role of the electrophile. The carbon of (CH₃)₃CBr is the electron-deficient site that is attacked; the donor, H₂O, is the nucleophile.
H₂O is the nucleophile, but not for this reason. The new C–O bond is made from a lone pair on oxygen; the carbon supplies no electrons.
The O atom of water has lone pairs; one is donated to the electron-deficient carbon atom, forming the C–O bond of the alcohol. A neutral molecule can be a nucleophile.

mcqs.q: 1-bromopropane is warmed with aqueous sodium hydroxide. Which equation represents the reaction that occurs?
options: CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂CH₂⁻ + HOBr
CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + Br⁻
CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂CHBr⁻ + H₂O
CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂CH₂OH⁻ + Br
mcqs.specStatementText: In a nucleophilic substitution reaction, a nucleophile donates an electron pair to form a new bond, as another bond breaks producing a leaving group.
mcqs.explain: OH⁻ donates a lone pair to the δ+ carbon bonded to Br, and the C–Br bonding pair leaves with Br as the bromide ion. The product is propan-1-ol.
rationales: This has OH⁻ bonding to the bromine atom. Br is the δ− end of the C–Br bond; an electron-rich nucleophile is attracted to the δ+ carbon, so the C–O bond forms and Br⁻ leaves.
OH⁻ donates a lone pair to the δ+ carbon bonded to Br, and the C–Br bonding pair leaves with Br as the bromide ion. The product is propan-1-ol.
This treats OH⁻ as a base removing H⁺ from carbon. With a halogenoalkane, OH⁻ acts as a nucleophile: it donates its lone pair to the carbon bonded to Br, substituting for the halogen.

This splits the C–Br bonding pair one electron to each atom, so Br leaves as an atom. In substitution the C–Br bond breaks heterolytically: Br takes both electrons and leaves as Br⁻, and the alcohol is neutral.

mcqs.q: In the reaction CH₃CH₂Br + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂OH + Br⁻ a new C–O bond forms. Where do the two electrons of the new C–O bond come from?
options: One from the O atom and one from the C atom
Both from the C–Br bond, which becomes the new C–O bond
Both from a lone pair on the O atom of the OH⁻ ion
Both from the C atom, which donates them to the O
mcqs.specStatementText: In a nucleophilic substitution reaction, a nucleophile donates an electron pair to form a new bond, as another bond breaks producing a leaving group.
mcqs.explain: OH⁻ is the nucleophile: a lone pair on its oxygen is donated to the δ+ carbon and becomes the C–O bonding pair. The C–Br pair leaves with Br⁻.
rationales: Dot-and-cross diagrams show each atom giving one electron, but here the nucleophile supplies both. The carbon's electrons in the C–Br bond leave with Br⁻.
The C–Br pair is not handed over to O: it moves onto Br, which leaves as Br⁻ carrying both electrons. The new C–O pair is a lone pair donated by the O of OH⁻.
OH⁻ is the nucleophile: a lone pair on its oxygen is donated to the δ+ carbon and becomes the C–O bonding pair. The C–Br pair leaves with Br⁻.
This makes the halogenoalkane carbon the donor. The carbon is δ+ and electron-deficient, so it accepts the pair; the electron-rich OH⁻ donates it.

mcqs.q: Which statement describes the heterolytic fission of a covalent bond?
options: One bonding electron goes to each fragment, so radicals form.
Both bonding electrons go to one fragment, so two ions form.
Both bonding electrons go to one fragment, which becomes positive.
It is the breaking of a bond that joins two different elements.
mcqs.specStatementText: Heterolytic fission is the breakage of a covalent bond when both bonding electrons remain with one of the two fragments formed.
mcqs.explain: In heterolytic fission one fragment keeps the bonding pair and becomes an anion; the other becomes a cation, e.g. H–Br → H⁺ + Br⁻.
rationales: An even split of the bonding pair is homolytic fission, which gives radicals. Heterolytic fission gives both electrons to one fragment, forming ions.
In heterolytic fission one fragment keeps the bonding pair and becomes an anion; the other becomes a cation, e.g. H–Br → H⁺ + Br⁻.
A fragment that takes both electrons gains negative charge, so it becomes the anion. The fragment left without the pair becomes the cation.

'Hetero-' describes the two different fragments formed (a cation and an anion), not the atoms in the bond. A bond between different atoms can break either way: C–Cl breaks heterolytically when a nucleophile substitutes for Cl, but homolytically in UV light, giving radicals.

mcqs.q: Hydrogen chloride undergoes heterolytic fission to form H⁺ and Cl⁻. Which describes the curly arrow for this change?
options: It starts at the H–Cl bond and ends on the H atom.
It starts on the Cl atom and points back to the H–Cl bond.
It starts on the H atom and shows the H⁺ ion moving away.
It starts at the H–Cl bond and ends on the Cl atom.
mcqs.specStatementText: Heterolytic fission is the breakage of a covalent bond when both bonding electrons remain with one of the two fragments formed.
mcqs.explain: A curly arrow shows an electron pair moving from its source to its destination. The H–Cl bonding pair moves onto Cl, which becomes Cl⁻, leaving H⁺.
rationales: If the pair went to H, H would become H⁻ and Cl would become Cl⁺. The product H⁺ shows that H has lost its share of the pair, so the arrow ends on Cl.
An arrow starting on Cl and ending on the bond would show electrons moving INTO the bond, which forms a bond rather than breaking one. Start at the source of the pair: the H–Cl bond.
A curly arrow never shows an atom or ion moving; it shows an electron pair. The pair in the H–Cl bond moves to Cl, and H⁺ is what is left behind.
A curly arrow shows an electron pair moving from its source to its destination. The H–Cl bonding pair moves onto Cl, which becomes Cl⁻, leaving H⁺.

mcqs.q:
Ethene reacts with bromine:
CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → CH₂BrCH₂Br
Which reactant acts as the electrophile?
options: Br₂, as it accepts an electron pair from the C=C bond
Ethene, as its C=C bond is rich in electrons
Neither, as neither reactant carries a positive charge
Ethene, as its C atoms need electrons for an octet
mcqs.specStatementText: An electrophile is a reactant that forms a bond to its reaction partner (the nucleophile) by accepting both bonding electrons from that reaction partner.
mcqs.explain: Br₂ accepts the electron pair donated by the electron-rich C=C bond, forming a C–Br bond. A neutral molecule can be an electrophile.
rationales: Br₂ accepts the electron pair donated by the electron-rich C=C bond, forming a C–Br bond. A neutral molecule can be an electrophile.
It is true that the C=C bond is electron-rich, but that makes ethene the electron-pair DONOR, the nucleophile. The electrophile is the electron-pair acceptor, Br₂.
An electrophile need not be charged. Br₂ accepts an electron pair from the C=C bond, so it is the electrophile, even though it is neutral.
Each carbon in C=C already has an octet. The C=C bond is electron-rich and donates a pair; Br₂ accepts it, so Br₂ is the electrophile.

mcqs.q:
Ammonia reacts with hydrogen ions:
NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺
Which species acts as the electrophile?
options: NH₃, as its nitrogen atom carries a lone pair of electrons
Neither, as N and H each supply one electron to the bond
H⁺, as it accepts the lone pair on the nitrogen atom
H⁺, as it forms an ionic bond with the nitrogen atom of NH₃
mcqs.specStatementText: An electrophile is a reactant that forms a bond to its reaction partner (the nucleophile) by accepting both bonding electrons from that reaction partner.
mcqs.explain: H⁺ has no electrons and accepts the lone pair of nitrogen to form the new N–H bond. A positively charged species that accepts a pair is an electrophile.
rationales: Having a lone pair to donate makes NH₃ the nucleophile (the electron-pair donor). The electrophile is the acceptor, H⁺.
H⁺ has no electrons, so it cannot supply one. Both electrons of the new N–H bond come from the nitrogen lone pair; H⁺ accepts them and is the electrophile.
H⁺ has no electrons and accepts the lone pair of nitrogen to form the new N–H bond. A positively charged species that accepts a pair is an electrophile.
H⁺ is the electrophile, but the bond it forms is covalent: the nitrogen lone pair is shared between N and H. NH₄⁺ has four identical covalent N–H bonds.

mcqs.q: Why are alkenes susceptible to attack by electrophiles?
options: The C=C double bond is weaker than a C–C single bond.
The C=C double bond is a region of high electron density.
The carbon atoms of C=C are deficient in electrons.
The C=C carbon atoms need more electrons for an octet.
mcqs.specStatementText: Alkenes are susceptible to electrophilic attack because of the high electron density of the carbon–carbon double bond. These reactions lead to electrophilic addition.
mcqs.explain: The double bond concentrates electron density between and around the two carbon atoms, and this electron-rich region attracts electron-pair acceptors.
rationales: C=C is stronger than C–C (it has a higher bond enthalpy). Alkenes react because of the high electron density of the double bond, not because it is weak.
The double bond concentrates electron density between and around the two carbon atoms, and this electron-rich region attracts electron-pair acceptors.
An electrophile seeks electrons, so it attacks an electron-RICH site. The carbon atoms of C=C are surrounded by high electron density, not a deficit.
Each carbon in C=C shares four electron pairs and already has an octet. The reason is the high electron density of the double bond.

mcqs.q: Ethene is bubbled through a solution of bromine in an organic solvent at room temperature, in the dark. Which statement is correct?
options: The bromine loses its colour as CH₂BrCH₂Br forms by addition.
The bromine loses its colour as CH₂=CHBr forms by substitution.
No reaction occurs, as Br₂ has no positive charge.
No reaction occurs, as UV light is needed to split Br₂.
mcqs.specStatementText: Alkenes are susceptible to electrophilic attack because of the high electron density of the carbon–carbon double bond. These reactions lead to electrophilic addition.
mcqs.explain: Br₂ adds across the C=C bond: CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → CH₂BrCH₂Br. The orange-brown colour of bromine disappears; this is the test for C=C.
rationales: Br₂ adds across the C=C bond: CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → CH₂BrCH₂Br. The orange-brown colour of bromine disappears; this is the test for C=C.
Replacing an H atom and keeping C=C is how alkanes react (with UV light). Alkenes react by addition, and the product 1,2-dibromoethane has no C=C bond.
An electrophile need not be positive. Neutral Br₂ accepts an electron pair from the C=C bond, so the reaction occurs and the colour disappears.
UV light is needed for radical substitution of alkanes. Alkenes react with Br₂ rapidly in the dark, which is why bromine is used to test for C=C.

mcqs.q: But-2-ene, CH₃CH=CHCH₃, undergoes hydration when heated with steam in the presence of an acid catalyst. Which statement is correct?
options: Water adds across the C=C bond, forming butane-2,3-diol.
An OH group replaces an H atom, forming but-2-en-2-ol.
H atoms from water add across C=C, forming butane.
Water adds across the C=C bond, forming butan-2-ol.
mcqs.specStatementText: Alkenes are susceptible to electrophilic attack because of the high electron density of the carbon–carbon double bond. These reactions lead to electrophilic addition.
mcqs.explain: H adds to one carbon of C=C and OH to the other: CH₃CH=CHCH₃ + H₂O → CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃, butan-2-ol.
rationales: A diol would need an OH group on both carbons, but water supplies only one OH. One carbon receives H and the other OH, giving butan-2-ol.
Alkenes react by addition, not substitution. The C=C bond becomes a single bond as H and OH add across it, giving butan-2-ol.
Adding hydrogen to form an alkane is hydrogenation (H₂ with a catalyst). Hydration adds both parts of water, H and OH, giving butan-2-ol.
H adds to one carbon of C=C and OH to the other: CH₃CH=CHCH₃ + H₂O → CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃, butan-2-ol.

mcqs.q: Ethene is mixed with hydrogen bromide gas at room temperature. Which statement is correct?
options: HBr adds across the C=C bond, forming CH₂BrCH₂Br.
A Br atom replaces one H atom, forming CH₂=CHBr.
HBr adds across the C=C bond, forming CH₃CH₂Br.
No reaction occurs, as the HBr molecule is neutral.
mcqs.specStatementText: Alkenes are susceptible to electrophilic attack because of the high electron density of the carbon–carbon double bond. These reactions lead to electrophilic addition.
mcqs.explain: H adds to one carbon and Br to the other: CH₂=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃CH₂Br, bromoethane.
rationales: HBr has only one Br atom, so it cannot put Br on both carbons. One carbon gains H and the other gains Br, giving CH₃CH₂Br.
Substitution that keeps C=C is not how alkenes react. HBr adds across the double bond, giving CH₃CH₂Br with no C=C bond.
H adds to one carbon and Br to the other: CH₂=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃CH₂Br, bromoethane.
A neutral molecule can be an electrophile. HBr accepts an electron pair from the C=C bond at its δ+ H atom, and bromoethane forms.

mcqs.q:
Aluminium chloride reacts with chloride ions:
AlCl₃ + Cl⁻ → AlCl₄⁻
Which statement identifies the Lewis acid in this reaction?
options: Cl⁻, as it donates an electron pair to AlCl₃
AlCl₃, as it accepts an electron pair from Cl⁻
Neither, as no H⁺ ion is transferred at all
AlCl₃, as Al forms an ionic bond with Cl⁻
mcqs.specStatementText: A Lewis acid is an electron-pair acceptor and a Lewis base is an electron-pair donor.
mcqs.explain: Al in AlCl₃ has only six outer electrons and accepts a lone pair from Cl⁻, forming a coordination bond in AlCl₄⁻. An electron-pair acceptor is a Lewis acid.
rationales: Donating the electron pair makes Cl⁻ the Lewis BASE. In Lewis theory the acid is the acceptor, AlCl₃.
Al in AlCl₃ has only six outer electrons and accepts a lone pair from Cl⁻, forming a coordination bond in AlCl₄⁻. An electron-pair acceptor is a Lewis acid.
That is the Brønsted–Lowry test. Lewis theory needs no hydrogen: AlCl₃ accepts an electron pair, so it is a Lewis acid.
AlCl₃ is the Lewis acid, but not because an ionic bond forms. The Cl⁻ lone pair is shared with Al in a covalent coordination bond.

mcqs.q: In the first step of the acid-catalysed addition of water to ethene, H⁺ bonds to one carbon atom of the C=C bond, forming CH₃CH₂⁺. Which species acts as the Lewis base in this step?
options: Neither, as ethene has no lone pair to donate
H⁺, as it accepts the electron pair of the C=C bond
Ethene, as its C=C electrons form the new C–H bond
Ethene, as it gives two electrons to H⁺ in an ionic bond
mcqs.specStatementText: A Lewis acid is an electron-pair acceptor and a Lewis base is an electron-pair donor.
mcqs.explain: The electron pair of the second bond of C=C is donated to H⁺ and becomes the new C–H bond. The electron-pair donor, ethene, is the Lewis base; H⁺ is the Lewis acid.
rationales: A Lewis base needs an available electron pair, not necessarily a lone pair. The electron pair of the C=C second bond is donated to H⁺.
Accepting an electron pair makes H⁺ the Lewis ACID. The Lewis base is the donor, ethene.
The electron pair of the second bond of C=C is donated to H⁺ and becomes the new C–H bond. The electron-pair donor, ethene, is the Lewis base; H⁺ is the Lewis acid.
Ethene is the Lewis base, but the bond formed is covalent: the donated pair is shared between C and H in the new C–H bond.

mcqs.q: Ammonia reacts with boron trifluoride to form H₃NBF₃. The Lewis formula of the product is often drawn with a positive formal charge on N and a negative formal charge on B. Which statement about the new N–B bond is correct?
options: It is a coordination bond; both electrons came from N
It is a coordination bond; both of its electrons came from B
It is a covalent bond; N and B each gave an electron
It is an ionic bond, as N carries + and B carries −
mcqs.specStatementText: When a Lewis base reacts with a Lewis acid, a coordination bond is formed. Nucleophiles are Lewis bases and electrophiles are Lewis acids.
mcqs.explain: N in NH₃ has a lone pair and B in BF₃ has only six outer electrons. N donates its lone pair to B, forming a coordination bond; the formal charges record this donation.
rationales: N in NH₃ has a lone pair and B in BF₃ has only six outer electrons. N donates its lone pair to B, forming a coordination bond; the formal charges record this donation.
BF₃ is the Lewis acid, the acceptor. B has no lone pair to donate; the pair comes from the nitrogen of NH₃, the Lewis base.
Each atom giving one electron is the dot-and-cross picture of an ordinary covalent bond. Here both electrons come from the N lone pair, so it is a coordination bond.
The + and − are formal charges in one molecule, not the charges of separate ions. N and B share the donated pair, so the bond is covalent (coordination).

mcqs.q: In the reaction CH₃CH₂Br + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂OH + Br⁻, which statement about OH⁻ is correct?
options: It is a nucleophile, and so it is a Lewis acid.
It is an electrophile, as it is rich in electrons.
It is a nucleophile but no base, as it gains no H⁺.
It is a nucleophile, and so it is also a Lewis base.
mcqs.specStatementText: When a Lewis base reacts with a Lewis acid, a coordination bond is formed. Nucleophiles are Lewis bases and electrophiles are Lewis acids.
mcqs.explain: OH⁻ donates a lone pair to the carbon atom. Every nucleophile is an electron-pair donor, so it is also a Lewis base.
rationales: A Lewis acid accepts an electron pair. OH⁻ donates one, so as a nucleophile it is a Lewis BASE; electrophiles are the Lewis acids.
Being electron-rich makes OH⁻ a nucleophile, the electron-pair donor. An electrophile is electron-deficient and accepts a pair.
Gaining H⁺ is the Brønsted–Lowry test. In Lewis terms OH⁻ is a base because it donates an electron pair, which it does here.
OH⁻ donates a lone pair to the carbon atom. Every nucleophile is an electron-pair donor, so it is also a Lewis base.

mcqs.q: Which statement describes the bonding between H₂O and Cu²⁺ in the complex ion [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺?
options: Cu²⁺ donates an electron pair to each H₂O, forming a coordination bond.
Each H₂O donates a lone pair to Cu²⁺, forming a coordination bond.
Each H₂O is held to Cu²⁺ by an ionic bond, as Cu is a metal.
Each H₂O and the Cu²⁺ give one electron to form a covalent bond.
mcqs.specStatementText: Coordination bonds are formed when ligands donate an electron pair to transition element cations, forming complex ions.
mcqs.explain: Each water ligand donates a lone pair from its oxygen atom to Cu²⁺. Six coordination bonds form, and the ligands act as Lewis bases.
rationales: The metal cation is the electron-pair acceptor (Lewis acid). The donors are the ligands, each giving a lone pair from oxygen.
Each water ligand donates a lone pair from its oxygen atom to Cu²⁺. Six coordination bonds form, and the ligands act as Lewis bases.
'Metal + non-metal = ionic' does not apply here. Each H₂O donates a lone pair that is shared with Cu²⁺, forming a covalent coordination bond.
In a coordination bond both electrons come from one atom. Here the oxygen of each water supplies both; Cu²⁺ supplies none.

mcqs.q: A complex ion contains one Cr³⁺ ion, four H₂O ligands and two Cl⁻ ligands. What is the charge on the complex ion [CrCl₂(H₂O)₄]?
mcqs.specStatementText: Coordination bonds are formed when ligands donate an electron pair to transition element cations, forming complex ions.
mcqs.explain: Charge = (+3) + 2(−1) + 4(0) = +1. The Cl⁻ ligands each add −1 and the neutral water ligands add nothing, so the complex is [CrCl₂(H₂O)₄]⁺.
mcqs.working: Charge on complex = charge on metal ion + sum of ligand charges = (+3) + 2 × (−1) + 4 × 0 = +1, so the ion is [CrCl₂(H₂O)₄]⁺.
rationales: This is the charge of the metal ion alone. The two Cl⁻ ligands each carry −1, so the complex charge is (+3) + 2(−1) = +1.
This counts every ligand as −1: (+3) + 6(−1) = −3. Water is neutral, so only the two Cl⁻ ligands contribute: (+3) + 2(−1) = +1.
This adds the sizes of the charges, 3 + 2 = 5, ignoring the negative sign of Cl⁻. Algebraically, (+3) + 2(−1) = +1.
Charge = (+3) + 2(−1) + 4(0) = +1. The Cl⁻ ligands each add −1 and the neutral water ligands add nothing, so the complex is [CrCl₂(H₂O)₄]⁺.

mcqs.q: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, (CH₃)₃CBr, reacts with aqueous hydroxide ions by the SN1 mechanism. Which describes the first step?
options: The C–Br bond breaks heterolytically, forming (CH₃)₃C⁺ and Br⁻.
OH⁻ attacks the C atom as the C–Br bond breaks, in a single step.
The C–Br bond breaks homolytically, giving radicals (CH₃)₃C• and Br•.
The C–Br bond breaks heterolytically, forming (CH₃)₃C⁻ and Br⁺ ions.
mcqs.specStatementText: Nucleophilic substitution reactions include the reactions between halogenoalkanes and nucleophiles.
mcqs.explain: The slow first step of SN1 is heterolysis of C–Br: Br takes the bonding pair (curly arrow from the C–Br bond to Br), giving a tertiary carbocation and Br⁻. OH⁻ attacks the carbocation in the second, fast step.
rationales: The slow first step of SN1 is heterolysis of C–Br: Br takes the bonding pair (curly arrow from the C–Br bond to Br), giving a tertiary carbocation and Br⁻. OH⁻ attacks the carbocation in the second, fast step.
A single concerted step is the SN2 mechanism. The '1' in SN1 refers to one species in the rate-determining step; SN1 has two steps, starting with formation of the carbocation.
Substitution by a nucleophile involves heterolytic fission. Br, the more electronegative atom, takes both bonding electrons and leaves as Br⁻, forming a carbocation, not radicals.
Br takes the bonding pair, and gaining the pair makes it negative: Br⁻. The carbon, having lost its share, becomes positive: (CH₃)₃C⁺.

mcqs.q: A single enantiomer of 2-bromobutane, CH₃CHBrCH₂CH₃, reacts with aqueous hydroxide ions by the SN2 mechanism. Which statement about this reaction is correct?
options: OH⁻ takes the exact place of Br, so the configuration is retained.
A carbocation forms first, so a racemic mixture is produced.
OH⁻ attacks opposite Br, so the configuration is inverted.
A stable five-bonded intermediate forms, then Br⁻ leaves.
mcqs.specStatementText: Nucleophilic substitution reactions include the reactions between halogenoalkanes and nucleophiles.
mcqs.explain: In SN2 the nucleophile approaches the δ+ carbon from the side opposite the leaving group. As Br⁻ leaves, the other three groups flip over, so a single enantiomer of butan-2-ol forms with inverted configuration: SN2 is stereospecific.
rationales: Substitution is not a same-side swap. The nucleophile must approach from the back, away from Br, so the configuration is inverted.
A carbocation forms in SN1, not SN2. The '2' means two species in the rate-determining step; SN2 is one concerted step with no carbocation, so a single inverted enantiomer forms.

In SN2 the nucleophile approaches the δ+ carbon from the side opposite the leaving group. As Br⁻ leaves, the other three groups flip over, so a single enantiomer of butan-2-ol forms with inverted configuration: SN2 is stereospecific.
The five-coordinate species is a transition state, an energy maximum, not an intermediate that can exist. SN2 is a single step.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the mechanisms of nucleophilic substitution of halogenoalkanes is correct?
options: Secondary ones react by SN1 and SN2, as both paths are feasible.
Primary ones react by SN1, as their carbocations are most stable.
Tertiary ones react by SN1, which takes place in one step.
Primary ones react via a stable intermediate with five bonds to C.
mcqs.specStatementText: Nucleophilic substitution reactions include the reactions between halogenoalkanes and nucleophiles.
mcqs.explain: Primary halogenoalkanes react by SN2 and tertiary by SN1. A secondary carbocation is of intermediate stability and backside attack is only partly hindered, so both mechanisms occur.
rationales: Primary halogenoalkanes react by SN2 and tertiary by SN1. A secondary carbocation is of intermediate stability and backside attack is only partly hindered, so both mechanisms occur.
Primary carbocations are the LEAST stable, because alkyl groups release electrons and a primary carbon has only one. Primary halogenoalkanes react by SN2.
Tertiary halogenoalkanes do react by SN1, but SN1 has two steps: formation of the carbocation, then attack by the nucleophile. The '1' is not a count of steps.
Primary halogenoalkanes react by SN2, which has a transition state (an energy maximum), not a stable intermediate. The reaction is one step.

mcqs.q: 1-chlorobutane, 1-bromobutane and 1-iodobutane are each warmed with aqueous sodium hydroxide under identical conditions. Which reacts fastest, and why?
options: 1-chlorobutane, as its C–Cl bond is the most polar
1-iodobutane, as its C–I bond is the weakest
1-chlorobutane, as the small Cl blocks attack least
None; all react equally fast, as OH⁻ attacks C
mcqs.specStatementText: The rate of the substitution reactions is influenced by the identity of the leaving group.
mcqs.explain: The C–X bond must break for substitution to occur. Bond enthalpy falls from C–Cl to C–Br to C–I, so C–I breaks most easily and 1-iodobutane reacts fastest.
rationales: C–Cl is the most polar, but polarity is not what controls the rate here. The C–Cl bond is the strongest and the hardest to break, so 1-chlorobutane is the slowest.
The C–X bond must break for substitution to occur. Bond enthalpy falls from C–Cl to C–Br to C–I, so C–I breaks most easily and 1-iodobutane reacts fastest.
The size of the halogen is not what controls this rate. C–I is the weakest C–X bond and breaks most easily, so 1-iodobutane reacts fastest even though iodine is the largest.
OH⁻ does attack carbon, but the C–X bond must also break, and its strength depends on the halogen. The rates differ: iodo > bromo > chloro.

mcqs.q: Under identical conditions, which reacts faster with aqueous hydroxide ions, 1-bromobutane or 1-chlorobutane, and why?
options: 1-chlorobutane, as the C–Cl bond is more polar than C–Br
1-chlorobutane, as the smaller Cl atom blocks attack less
Neither; both react at the same rate, as OH⁻ attacks C
1-bromobutane, as the C–Br bond is weaker than the C–Cl bond
mcqs.specStatementText: The rate of the substitution reactions is influenced by the identity of the leaving group.
mcqs.explain: The C–Br bond enthalpy is lower than that of C–Cl, so it breaks more easily and bromide is the better leaving group. 1-bromobutane reacts faster.
rationales: C–Cl is more polar, but the rate is controlled by how easily the C–X bond breaks. C–Cl is stronger, so 1-chlorobutane reacts more slowly.
The nucleophile attacks from the side opposite the halogen, so the halogen's size does not block it. The weaker C–Br bond makes 1-bromobutane faster.
OH⁻ does attack carbon, but the C–X bond must also break, and its strength depends on the halogen. C–Br is weaker than C–Cl, so 1-bromobutane reacts faster.
The C–Br bond enthalpy is lower than that of C–Cl, so it breaks more easily and bromide is the better leaving group. 1-bromobutane reacts faster.

mcqs.q: Ethene reacts with hydrogen bromide by electrophilic addition. Which describes the curly arrows in the first step of the mechanism?
options: From the H atom of HBr to the C=C bond, and from Br to the H–Br bond
From the C=C bond to the Br of HBr, and from the H–Br bond to the H
From the C=C bond to the H of HBr, and from the H–Br bond to Br
Fish-hook arrows split H–Br into H• and Br•, which add to C=C
mcqs.specStatementText: Alkenes readily undergo electrophilic addition reactions.
mcqs.explain: The electron-rich C=C bond donates a pair to the δ+ H atom, forming a C–H bond, while the H–Br bonding pair moves onto Br. This gives CH₃CH₂⁺ and Br⁻; Br⁻ then bonds to the carbocation.
rationales: These arrows start at the electron-poor atoms. A curly arrow starts at the electron pair: at the C=C bond and at the H–Br bond.
Br is the δ− end of H–Br. The electron-rich C=C bond is attracted to the δ+ H, and the H–Br pair goes to the more electronegative Br, forming Br⁻.
The electron-rich C=C bond donates a pair to the δ+ H atom, forming a C–H bond, while the H–Br bonding pair moves onto Br. This gives CH₃CH₂⁺ and Br⁻; Br⁻ then bonds to the carbocation.
Electrophilic addition is not a radical reaction. The H–Br bond breaks heterolytically, Br taking the pair, while the C=C pair forms the C–H bond.

mcqs.q: Ethene reacts with bromine by electrophilic addition. How does the non-polar Br₂ molecule come to act as an electrophile?
options: Br₂ first ionizes into Br⁺ and Br⁻, and Br⁺ accepts the C=C electron pair.
UV light splits Br₂ into Br atoms, and each Br atom adds to a carbon.
One Br atom donates an electron pair to C=C, forming a C–Br bond.
The electron-rich C=C induces a dipole in Br₂, and Brδ+ accepts the C=C pair.
mcqs.specStatementText: Alkenes readily undergo electrophilic addition reactions.
mcqs.explain: As Br₂ approaches, the C=C electron density repels the Br–Br bonding pair, making the near Br δ+. A curly arrow from C=C to Brδ+ and one from Br–Br to Brδ− give a carbocation and Br⁻, which then bonds to it.
rationales: Br₂ does not need to ionize first: a neutral molecule can be an electrophile. The Br–Br bond is polarized by the approaching C=C bond and breaks as the C–Br bond forms.
UV light is needed for radical substitution of alkanes. Alkenes react with Br₂ in the dark by electrophilic addition, via an induced dipole and heterolytic fission.
Br₂ is the electrophile, so it accepts the pair; the C=C bond is the donor. The curly arrow goes from the C=C bond to the Brδ+ atom.

As Br₂ approaches, the C=C electron density repels the Br–Br bonding pair, making the near Br δ+. A curly arrow from C=C to Brδ+ and one from Br–Br to Brδ− give a carbocation and Br⁻, which then bonds to it.

mcqs.q: In the acid-catalysed addition of water to ethene, the first step forms the carbocation CH₃CH₂⁺. Which describes what happens next?
options: A lone pair on the O of H₂O bonds to C⁺, then H⁺ is lost, regenerating the catalyst.
A lone pair on the O of H₂O bonds to C⁺, and the H⁺ stays, so the acid is used up.
The C⁺ ion donates an electron pair to the O atom of H₂O, forming a C–O bond.
H₂O first ionizes to OH⁻, as only a negative ion can bond to the C⁺ ion.
mcqs.specStatementText: Alkenes readily undergo electrophilic addition reactions.
mcqs.explain: Water is the nucleophile: an O lone pair forms the C–O bond, giving CH₃CH₂OH₂⁺. This loses H⁺ (curly arrow from the O–H bond to O), giving ethanol and regenerating the H⁺ catalyst.
rationales: Water is the nucleophile: an O lone pair forms the C–O bond, giving CH₃CH₂OH₂⁺. This loses H⁺ (curly arrow from the O–H bond to O), giving ethanol and regenerating the H⁺ catalyst.
The first part is right, but the catalyst is not consumed. CH₃CH₂OH₂⁺ loses H⁺ to give ethanol, so the H⁺ used in the first step is regenerated.
The carbocation has an empty orbital and no pair to donate; it is the electrophile. The O atom of H₂O donates a lone pair to the positive carbon.
A neutral molecule with a lone pair can be a nucleophile. In the acidic mixture H₂O itself bonds to C⁺; OH⁻ is not needed.

mcqs.q: Propene, CH₃CH=CH₂, reacts with hydrogen bromide. What is the major product, and why?
options: 1-bromopropane, as H adds to the carbon that has fewer H atoms
2-bromopropane, as it forms via the more stable secondary carbocation
1-bromopropane, as it forms via the more stable primary carbocation
Equal amounts of both, as H adds to either carbon atom with equal chance
mcqs.specStatementText: The relative stability of carbocations in the addition reactions between hydrogen halides and unsymmetrical alkenes can be used to explain the reaction mechanism.
mcqs.explain: H adds to the CH₂ end, giving the secondary carbocation CH₃CH⁺CH₃, stabilized by two electron-releasing alkyl groups. Br⁻ bonds to it, giving mainly 2-bromopropane.
rationales: The rule is reversed. H adds to the carbon with MORE H atoms (the CH₂ end) because that gives the more stable secondary carbocation, so Br ends up on C2.
H adds to the CH₂ end, giving the secondary carbocation CH₃CH⁺CH₃, stabilized by two electron-releasing alkyl groups. Br⁻ bonds to it, giving mainly 2-bromopropane.
Primary carbocations are the least stable: alkyl groups release electrons, and a primary carbon has only one. The secondary carbocation forms, giving 2-bromopropane.
The two directions give carbocations of different stability. The secondary carbocation forms much faster, so 2-bromopropane is the major product.

mcqs.q: 2-methylpropene, (CH₃)₂C=CH₂, reacts with water in the presence of an acid catalyst. What is the major organic product?
options: 2-methylpropan-1-ol, as H adds to the C with fewer H
2-methylpropane-1,2-diol, as OH adds to each carbon
2-methylpropan-2-ol, via the tertiary carbocation
A 1:1 mixture of the two possible alcohols
mcqs.specStatementText: The relative stability of carbocations in the addition reactions between hydrogen halides and unsymmetrical alkenes can be used to explain the reaction mechanism.
mcqs.explain: H⁺ adds to the CH₂ end, giving the tertiary carbocation (CH₃)₃C⁺, the most stable possible. Water bonds to it and loses H⁺, giving mainly (CH₃)₃COH.
rationales: H⁺ adds to the carbon with MORE H atoms (CH₂), so that the tertiary carbocation forms. OH then ends up on the central carbon: 2-methylpropan-2-ol.
Water supplies one H and one OH, not two OH groups. H adds to one carbon and OH to the other, giving 2-methylpropan-2-ol as the major product.
H⁺ adds to the CH₂ end, giving the tertiary carbocation (CH₃)₃C⁺, the most stable possible. Water bonds to it and loses H⁺, giving mainly (CH₃)₃COH.
The two possible carbocations differ greatly in stability: tertiary vs primary. The tertiary one forms far faster, so 2-methylpropan-2-ol is the major product.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the reaction of benzene with electrophiles is correct?
options: It undergoes addition across a C=C bond, in the same way as an alkene.
It does not react at all, as its ring is saturated, like a cycloalkane.
It undergoes substitution in a single step, with no intermediate ion formed.
It undergoes substitution; the product keeps the delocalized ring.
mcqs.specStatementText: Electrophilic substitution reactions include the reactions of benzene with electrophiles.
mcqs.explain: Benzene's delocalized π ring is especially stable. Substitution replaces an H atom and restores the ring, whereas addition would destroy it.
rationales: Benzene has a delocalized ring, not three separate C=C bonds. Addition would destroy the delocalization, so benzene reacts by substitution.
Benzene is unsaturated and reacts with strong electrophiles such as NO₂⁺, by substitution. Its stability changes the type of reaction, not whether it reacts.
Substitution is not a direct swap. E⁺ first bonds to the ring, forming a positive intermediate; H⁺ is then lost to restore the delocalized ring.
Benzene's delocalized π ring is especially stable. Substitution replaces an H atom and restores the ring, whereas addition would destroy it.

mcqs.q: Benzene reacts with a charged electrophile, E⁺. Which sequence describes the mechanism?
options: Ring π electrons bond to E⁺, forming a cation; loss of H⁺ restores the ring.
Ring π electrons bond to E⁺, forming a cation; a nucleophile then adds to it.
E⁺ donates an electron pair to the ring, forming an anion; H⁻ is then lost.
E⁺ swaps directly with an H atom in one step; the ring stays delocalized.
mcqs.specStatementText: Electrophilic substitution reactions include the reactions of benzene with electrophiles.
mcqs.explain: A curly arrow from the delocalized ring to E⁺ forms the C–E bond and a positive intermediate. A curly arrow from the C–H bond into the ring then releases H⁺ and restores delocalization: C₆H₆ + E⁺ → C₆H₅E + H⁺.
rationales: A curly arrow from the delocalized ring to E⁺ forms the C–E bond and a positive intermediate. A curly arrow from the C–H bond into the ring then releases H⁺ and restores delocalization: C₆H₆ + E⁺ → C₆H₅E + H⁺.
Adding a nucleophile completes an alkene-style addition and would leave the ring non-aromatic. Benzene's intermediate loses H⁺ instead, restoring the stable ring.
E⁺ is the electrophile, so it accepts an electron pair from the ring. The intermediate is a cation, and it loses H⁺, not H⁻.
Substitution is not a one-step swap. E⁺ first bonds to the ring, forming a cation in which delocalization is partly broken; H⁺ is then lost.

mcqs.q: 1-bromobutane, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂Br, and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, (CH₃)₃CBr, are each warmed with aqueous hydroxide ions. Which statement about their mechanisms is correct?
options: 1-bromobutane reacts by SN1 via a primary carbocation; (CH₃)₃CBr by SN2 in a single step
1-bromobutane reacts by SN2 in two separate steps; (CH₃)₃CBr by SN1 in a single step
1-bromobutane reacts by SN2 in a single step; (CH₃)₃CBr by SN1 via a carbocation
1-bromobutane reacts by SN2 via a stable intermediate; (CH₃)₃CBr by SN1 via a carbocation
mcqs.specStatementText: Nucleophilic substitution reactions include the reactions between halogenoalkanes and nucleophiles.
mcqs.explain: The primary halogenoalkane reacts by SN2: OH⁻ attacks the δ+ carbon from the side opposite Br as the C–Br bond breaks, in one concerted step through a transition state. The tertiary one reacts by SN1: its three methyl groups hinder attack from the back, and C–Br breaks first to give the stable tertiary carbocation (CH₃)₃C⁺, which OH⁻ then attacks.
rationales: Primary carbocations are the least stable: alkyl groups release electrons, and a primary carbon has only one. So 1-bromobutane reacts by one-step SN2, and (CH₃)₃CBr, which forms the stable tertiary carbocation, reacts by SN1.

The mechanisms are matched to the right compounds, but the step counts are reversed. The 2 in SN2 means two species in the rate-determining step of a one-step reaction; SN1 has two steps, carbocation formation and then attack by OH⁻.

The primary halogenoalkane reacts by SN2: OH⁻ attacks the δ+ carbon from the side opposite Br as the C–Br bond breaks, in one concerted step through a transition state. The tertiary one reacts by SN1: its three methyl groups hinder attack from the back, and C–Br breaks first to give the stable tertiary carbocation (CH₃)₃C⁺, which OH⁻ then attacks.
The tertiary part is right, but the five-coordinate species in SN2 is a transition state, an energy maximum, not an intermediate that can exist. SN2 of 1-bromobutane is a single step.

mcqs.q: Water can undergo heterolytic fission of one O–H bond to form H⁺ and OH⁻. The diagram shows four attempts, P to S, to draw this change with a curly arrow. Which drawing is correct?
options: Drawing Q
Drawing P
Drawing R
Drawing S
mcqs.specStatementText: Heterolytic fission is the breakage of a covalent bond when both bonding electrons remain with one of the two fragments formed.
mcqs.explain: A curly arrow starts where the electron pair is (the H–OH bond) and ends where it goes. Both bonding electrons go to oxygen, so OH takes the pair and becomes OH⁻, leaving H with no electrons: H⁺.
rationales: This arrow sends the bonding pair to H, which would form H⁻ and OH⁺. Gaining the pair makes a fragment negative, not positive, so to form OH⁻ the pair must go to the OH group.
A curly arrow starts where the electron pair is (the H–OH bond) and ends where it goes. Both bonding electrons go to oxygen, so OH takes the pair and becomes OH⁻, leaving H with no electrons: H⁺.

Each fish-hook arrow moves ONE electron, so R shows homolytic fission: one electron to each fragment, giving the radicals H• and •OH, not ions. To form H⁺ and OH⁻ both electrons must go to OH, shown by a single double-barbed arrow from the bond to OH.
A curly arrow is drawn from the electrons, not from the atom that receives them. It starts at the H–OH bonding pair and ends on the OH group; it is not drawn from OH back toward the bond.

mcqs.q: The diagram shows the reactants in the reaction BF₃ + F⁻ → BF₄⁻, with a curly arrow. BF₃ is drawn as a displayed formula; all four lone pairs of F⁻ are shown. Which statement about the reaction is correct?
options: F⁻ is the Lewis acid, since it is the species that donates the electron pair
Neither species is an acid or a base, since no H⁺ ion is transferred
B and F each supply one electron to the new bond, as in the other three B–F bonds
F⁻ is the Lewis base, since it supplies both electrons of the coordination bond
mcqs.specStatementText: When a Lewis base reacts with a Lewis acid, a coordination bond is formed. Nucleophiles are Lewis bases and electrophiles are Lewis acids.
mcqs.explain: The arrow starts at a lone pair on F⁻ and ends on B, which has only six electrons and an empty orbital. F⁻ donates the pair (Lewis base), BF₃ accepts it (Lewis acid), and a bond in which both electrons come from one atom is a coordination bond.
rationales: A Lewis acid ACCEPTS an electron pair. F⁻ donates the pair shown by the arrow, so it is the Lewis base; BF₃, whose B atom accepts the pair, is the Lewis acid.
Lewis theory does not require hydrogen. Any electron-pair donor is a Lewis base and any acceptor a Lewis acid, so BF₃ (acceptor) and F⁻ (donor) are a Lewis acid–base pair.

The arrow starts at a lone pair on F⁻, so both electrons of the new bond come from F⁻; B contributes none. Once formed, this coordination bond is the same as the other B–F bonds, but its electrons came from one atom.

The arrow starts at a lone pair on F⁻ and ends on B, which has only six electrons and an empty orbital. F⁻ donates the pair (Lewis base), BF₃ accepts it (Lewis acid), and a bond in which both electrons come from one atom is a coordination bond.

mcqs.q: The diagram shows a complex ion of cobalt with its ligands, drawn inside square brackets with the overall charge of the ion outside. What is the charge on the cobalt ion in this complex?
mcqs.specStatementText: Coordination bonds are formed when ligands donate an electron pair to transition element cations, forming complex ions.
mcqs.explain: Count the ligand charges from the diagram: four neutral NH₃ and two Cl⁻ give −2 in total. For the overall charge to be +1 the metal must be +3: (+3) + 2(−1) + 4(0) = +1.
mcqs.working: Overall charge = charge on metal ion + sum of ligand charges. The diagram shows four NH₃ ligands (each 0), two Cl⁻ ligands (each −1) and an overall charge of +1: +1 = x + 4(0) + 2(−1), so x = +1 + 2 = +3. The ion is [CoCl₂(NH₃)₄]⁺ containing Co³⁺.
rationales: This takes the overall charge outside the brackets as the charge on the metal. The two Cl⁻ ligands contribute −2, so the cobalt ion must be +3 for the complex to be +1.
Count the ligand charges from the diagram: four neutral NH₃ and two Cl⁻ give −2 in total. For the overall charge to be +1 the metal must be +3: (+3) + 2(−1) + 4(0) = +1.
This counts all six ligands as −1: +1 + 6 = +7. Donating a lone pair does not give a ligand a charge; NH₃ is neutral, and only the two Cl⁻ ligands carry −1, so the metal is +3.
This adds the size of the Cl⁻ charges to the metal charge, x + 2 = +1, giving x = −1. Charges are combined with their signs: x + 2(−1) = +1, so x = +3.

mcqs.q: A primary halogenoalkane and a tertiary halogenoalkane each react with aqueous hydroxide ions. The diagram shows the energy profiles, P and Q, of the two reactions. Which statement is correct?
options: Q is for the tertiary halogenoalkane, as its dip is the carbocation intermediate
P is for the tertiary halogenoalkane, as its single peak shows a one-step mechanism
Q is for the primary halogenoalkane, as its carbocation is the more stable one
P is for the primary halogenoalkane, as its peak is the intermediate of the reaction
mcqs.specStatementText: Nucleophilic substitution reactions include the reactions between halogenoalkanes and nucleophiles.
mcqs.explain: Two peaks mean two steps with an intermediate between them. A tertiary halogenoalkane reacts by SN1: slow heterolysis of C–X gives a carbocation (the dip, high in energy but a real species), then OH⁻ attacks it. The one-peak profile P is the concerted SN2 reaction of a primary halogenoalkane.
rationales: Two peaks mean two steps with an intermediate between them. A tertiary halogenoalkane reacts by SN1: slow heterolysis of C–X gives a carbocation (the dip, high in energy but a real species), then OH⁻ attacks it. The one-peak profile P is the concerted SN2 reaction of a primary halogenoalkane.

A tertiary halogenoalkane reacts by SN1, and the '1' means one species in the rate-determining step, not one step. SN1 has two steps and so two peaks (profile Q); the single peak of P is the concerted SN2 reaction of the primary halogenoalkane.

Alkyl groups release electron density, so a primary carbocation is the LEAST stable and does not form. Primary halogenoalkanes react in one concerted step (profile P); tertiary ones form a tertiary carbocation (profile Q).

P is indeed the one-step SN2 profile of the primary halogenoalkane, but its peak is a transition state, not an intermediate. The species at the top has partial bonds to both OH and the halogen, exists only momentarily and cannot be isolated. An intermediate sits in a dip between two peaks, like the carbocation in Q.

mcqs.q: But-1-ene, CH₃CH₂CH=CH₂, reacts with hydrogen bromide. The diagram shows skeletal formulas of the two carbocations, P and Q, that could form when H⁺ adds to the C=C bond. Which statement is correct?
options: Q forms faster, as its positive carbon has only one electron-withdrawing alkyl group
Q forms, as the H atom adds to the carbon atom of C=C that has fewer H atoms
P forms faster, as its positive carbon is stabilized by two electron-releasing alkyl groups
P and Q form in equal amounts, since H⁺ can add to either carbon of C=C
mcqs.specStatementText: The relative stability of carbocations in the addition reactions between hydrogen halides and unsymmetrical alkenes can be used to explain the reaction mechanism.
mcqs.explain: In P the + is on a carbon bonded to two other carbons (a secondary carbocation, CH₃CH₂CH⁺CH₃); in Q it is on an end carbon bonded to one (primary). Alkyl groups release electron density towards the positive carbon, so P is more stable, forms faster, and gives the major product 2-bromobutane.
rationales: Alkyl groups release electron density to a positive carbon; they do not withdraw it. More alkyl groups mean a more stable carbocation, so the secondary carbocation P is favoured over the primary Q.
The rule runs the other way: H adds to the carbon with MORE hydrogen atoms (the CH₂ end), so that the positive charge sits on the more substituted carbon. That gives P, the secondary carbocation.

In P the + is on a carbon bonded to two other carbons (a secondary carbocation, CH₃CH₂CH⁺CH₃); in Q it is on an end carbon bonded to one (primary). Alkyl groups release electron density towards the positive carbon, so P is more stable, forms faster, and gives the major product 2-bromobutane.
The two directions of addition give carbocations of different stability. The secondary carbocation P has a much lower activation energy, so it forms far faster and 2-bromobutane is the major product.

mcqs.q: The diagram shows the intermediate formed when benzene reacts with an electrophile, E⁺, together with the curly arrow for the step that follows. What happens in the step shown?
options: A nucleophile adds to the positive carbon, giving an addition product
The C–H bonding pair moves into the ring, restoring delocalization, and H⁺ is lost
The C–H bond breaks homolytically, releasing a hydrogen atom, H•
The arrow shows the hydrogen atom moving to another carbon atom of the ring
mcqs.specStatementText: Electrophilic substitution reactions include the reactions of benzene with electrophiles.
mcqs.explain: The arrow starts at the C–H bond and ends in the ring. Both electrons of that bond re-enter the π system, so the six-carbon delocalization is restored, the ring loses its positive charge, and the hydrogen leaves without its electrons as H⁺: C₆H₆ + E⁺ → C₆H₅E + H⁺.
rationales: Benzene does not react like an alkene here. Adding a nucleophile would leave the ring permanently non-aromatic; instead the C–H pair returns to the ring, H⁺ is lost, and the stable delocalized ring is regained (substitution).

The arrow starts at the C–H bond and ends in the ring. Both electrons of that bond re-enter the π system, so the six-carbon delocalization is restored, the ring loses its positive charge, and the hydrogen leaves without its electrons as H⁺: C₆H₆ + E⁺ → C₆H₅E + H⁺.
The arrow is a double-barbed curly arrow, so it moves a PAIR of electrons: heterolytic fission. Both electrons of the C–H bond go into the ring and the hydrogen leaves as H⁺, not as a radical.
Curly arrows show electrons, not atoms, moving. This arrow moves the C–H bonding pair into the ring; the hydrogen does not move around the ring, it is lost as H⁺.

specStatements.text: A nucleophile is a reactant that forms a bond to its reaction partner (the electrophile) by donating both bonding electrons.
specStatements.guidance: Recognize nucleophiles in chemical reactions. Both neutral and negatively charged species should be included.

specStatements.text: In a nucleophilic substitution reaction, a nucleophile donates an electron pair to form a new bond, as another bond breaks producing a leaving group.
specStatements.guidance: Deduce equations with descriptions and explanations of the movement of electron pairs in nucleophilic substitution reactions. Further details of the mechanisms are not required at SL.

specStatements.text: Heterolytic fission is the breakage of a covalent bond when both bonding electrons remain with one of the two fragments formed.
specStatements.guidance: Explain, with equations, the formation of ions by heterolytic fission. Curly arrows should be used to show the movement of electron pairs during reactions.

specStatements.text: An electrophile is a reactant that forms a bond to its reaction partner (the nucleophile) by accepting both bonding electrons from that reaction partner.
specStatements.guidance: Recognize electrophiles in chemical reactions. Both neutral and positively-charged species should be included.

specStatements.text: Alkenes are susceptible to electrophilic attack because of the high electron density of the carbon–carbon double bond. These reactions lead to electrophilic addition.
specStatements.guidance: Deduce equations for the reactions of alkenes with water, halogens, and hydrogen halides. The mechanisms of these reactions will not be assessed at SL.

specStatements.text: A Lewis acid is an electron-pair acceptor and a Lewis base is an electron-pair donor.
specStatements.guidance: Apply Lewis acid–base theory to inorganic and organic chemistry to identify the role of the reacting species.

specStatements.text: When a Lewis base reacts with a Lewis acid, a coordination bond is formed. Nucleophiles are Lewis bases and electrophiles are Lewis acids.
specStatements.guidance: Draw and interpret Lewis formulas of reactants and products to show coordination bond formation in Lewis acid–base reactions.

specStatements.text: Coordination bonds are formed when ligands donate an electron pair to transition element cations, forming complex ions.
specStatements.guidance: Deduce the charge on a complex ion, given the formula of the ion and ligands present.

specStatements.text: Nucleophilic substitution reactions include the reactions between halogenoalkanes and nucleophiles.

specStatements.text: The rate of the substitution reactions is influenced by the identity of the leaving group.

specStatements.guidance: Describe and explain the mechanisms of the reactions between symmetrical alkenes and halogens, water and hydrogen halides.

specStatements.text: The relative stability of carbocations in the addition reactions between hydrogen halides and unsymmetrical alkenes can be used to explain the reaction mechanism.

Curly-arrow mechanisms, induced dipoles and carbocations for these reactions are tested only on HL statements (R3.4.6, R3.4.11, R3.4.12).
